headline: High-risk filesystem overlap and default code-execution make the pair unsafe for shared-project use; prompt-injection and leakage are secondary but real.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: gpt-engineer writes files in a shared project directory and can execute generated code; pdf.js reads PDF files and runs in a browser-based worker. If pdf.js output or extracted text is copied into the project, malicious PDF content could be treated as instructions by gpt-engineer. The pathway is interaction-based and plausible, though not automatic.
conditions: IF pdf.js-derived text is copied into gpt-engineer prompts or files
IF the project directory contains attacker-controlled PDF content that gpt-engineer later reads as instructions
mitigations: Keep PDF-derived text out of prompt files
Use a separate staging directory for PDFs
Add a manual review step before copying extracted text
Disable auto-ingestion of project files into prompts
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to imported text

B_data_leakage.rationale: gpt-engineer has broad network egress and handles OPENAI_API_KEY, while pdf.js is local-only with no network egress. If both share a project directory, generated code or copied PDF contents can flow from pdf.js into gpt-engineer and then to a third-party model backend. The leakage path exists in default use and can expose document contents.
conditions: IF PDF contents are copied into the shared project directory
IF gpt-engineer sends those contents to its configured model backend
mitigations: Store PDFs outside the shared project directory
Redact sensitive text before prompting gpt-engineer
Use a local-only model for the coding agent
Rotate or scope API keys narrowly
requires-engineering: isolate per-agent workspaces

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can operate on files in the same project/workspace, and gpt-engineer has write_filesystem while pdf.js reads PDF files. Even without git writes, concurrent edits or file replacement can race in the shared directory and corrupt outputs. The overlap is real in default multi-instance use, though not as severe as unrestricted shared git mutation.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same project directory
IF pdf.js writes or replaces files that gpt-engineer is also editing
mitigations: Assign separate working directories
Serialize access to shared files
Use read-only mounts for pdf.js
Snapshot the workspace before each run
requires-engineering: add file-locking around shared paths

D_cascading_error.rationale: gpt-engineer can generate code and offer to run it, while pdf.js processes PDFs that may become source material for that code. If pdf.js output is treated as authoritative, gpt-engineer may propagate extraction errors into generated code or actions. The pair lacks a built-in verification boundary in the profiles, so cascading mistakes are plausible.
conditions: IF pdf.js extraction results are used as facts for code generation
IF gpt-engineer executes or commits code derived from unverified PDF text
mitigations: Require human verification of extracted facts
Keep source PDFs and generated code separate
Run generated code only after review
Annotate extracted text with confidence labels
requires-engineering: add a verification gate between agents

E_compliance.rationale: No explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented for either open-source agent. gpt-engineer handles generated source code and may transmit prompts to a configured model backend, while pdf.js touches PDF documents locally. Because the profiles do not show a concrete compliance conflict, only a low residual risk is justified.
conditions: IF regulated PDF content is entered into gpt-engineer and sent to a third-party backend
IF an operator imposes retention rules that differ between the two tools
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in prompts
Use local inference for sensitive documents
Document retention expectations for both tools
Delete temporary exports after use
requires-engineering: formalize residency and retention controls
